title: Why Dick Smith Shut His Food Brand While It Still Made Money
dek: In July 2018 Dick Smith announced he would wind down his Australian-owned food brand within a year, before he believed Aldi would finish it off.

story.event: Announcing the wind-down of a profitable but shrinking Australian-owned grocery brand
story.summary: Dick Smith founded Dick Smith Foods in 1999 to sell Australian-made food under licence from Australian-owned manufacturers, saying its profits went to charity. On 26 July 2018, with turnover down to about $15 million a year, he announced it would be wound down over twelve months while still profitable, blaming competition from Aldi. Suppliers were allowed to take over brands such as OzEmite.
paragraphs: On Thursday 26 July 2018, Dick Smith, then 74, told reporters in Sydney that he was closing the food brand that carried his name. Dick Smith Foods was still profitable, he said, but he did not think it would last more than another two years, so it would be wound down over the next twelve months. "In two years' time we will go out of business, so I'm closing it down now when times are good."

He had founded it in 1999, angry that Australian brands kept passing to foreign owners. What moved him, he said in 2018, was that Vegemite belonged to Kraft, which was then owned by the cigarette maker Philip Morris. The company made nothing itself: it licensed its name and labels to Australian-owned manufacturers, and Smith said its profits went to charity. Its first product, a peanut butter, soon took about a fifth of the national market. A trade journal noted in 2001 that much of the brand's growth seemed to come at the expense of other Australian-owned firms rather than the multinationals.

By mid-2018 the business had shrunk. In June Smith told The Land that it had once turned over $60 million a year and was down to $15 million or $16 million. He blamed Aldi, the German discount chain, for buying worldwide at the lowest price and running its stores with far fewer staff; the last straw, he said, was a survey naming Aldi the most trusted brand in Australia. The closure was forced on him, he said, because "most people just want the cheapest prices." He called it one of the saddest days of his life, and said that in this attempt to help farmers he had failed.

Only three people worked directly for the company, but its 13 remaining products came from suppliers in Victoria, Queensland and Tasmania. Smith let those suppliers take over brands such as OzEmite and OzEnuts, while worrying that they would need imported ingredients to compete. Aldi replied that it worked with more than 1,000 Australian suppliers. Over 19 years, Smith said, the brand had brought in about A$480 million in retail sales and given more than A$10 million to charity.

quote.text: She stirs up even the shiftless to toil; for a man grows eager to work when he considers his neighbour, a rich man who hastens to plough and plant and put his house in good order; and neighbour vies with his neighbour as he hurries after wealth. This Strife is wholesome for men.
quote.source_title: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, tr. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg eBook #348
quote.connection: Hesiod calls rivalry between neighbours a wholesome strife, the kind that makes even the idle work harder. Smith saw Aldi's competition as the other, harmful kind. Shoppers reaching for the cheaper jar were making their own judgement. The story does not settle whose reading was right.

reflection: There is a particular dignity in closing something while it still works. Smith could have kept going until the money ran out. He chose a date, told his suppliers, and let them keep the brands. Whatever you make of his argument about Aldi, the timing was a decision, not an accident.

He also called it a failure, out loud, after a long and very public career. Naming a failure plainly can be part of finishing well. If something in your own life is quietly winding down, you are allowed to decide when it ends, rather than waiting until it decides for you.
invitation: Pick one commitment that is still running but no longer feels like yours. Choose a date by which you will either renew it or let it go, and write that date down.

sources.title: Dick Smith Foods closing due to Aldi (Dean Blake, 26 July 2018)
sources.supports: Still profitable but expected to become unprofitable within two years; wind-down over 12 months; 'one of the saddest days in my life'; the company set up to help Australian farmers and food processors and Smith's statement that in this case he had failed; suppliers given permission to take over brands such as OzEmite and OzEnuts, and his worry about overseas ingredients; the open letter to Aldi's owners the day before

sources.title: Dick Smith Foods to close amid pressure from Aldi (news.com.au, 26 July 2018)

sources.title: Dick Smith Foods hitting its use-by date (Daniel Pedersen, 15 June 2018)

sources.title: How Dick Smith's business empire trades on patriotism (David Salter, 9 May 2012)

research_notes: Charity share disagrees: just-food (2001) reported a plan to return one third of profits to charity; news.com.au (2018) says the company donates its profits to charity; SmartCompany (2012) says only an undisclosed percentage was donated. The story says 'Smith said its profits went to charity' and gives his 2018 figure of more than A$10 million as his claim. Turnover: just-food (2001) gave revenues of A$90 million early on, while Smith told The Land in 2018 that the business had once turned over $60 million a year and was down to $15-16 million; these may be different measures (retail sales against company turnover), so the story uses only Smith's 2018 figures, attributed to him, and the A$480 million lifetime retail sales he gave at the closure. Profitability: SBS and Inside Retail report Smith saying the brand was still profitable; Wikipedia's article says it closed to avoid bankruptcy, which no source I could read supports, so the story follows the contemporary reports. Founding date: the National Portrait Gallery gives 1999 and the 2018 reports '19 years'; just-food, dated June 2001, says the first product launched 'in February last year', which would be 2000 (the archive date may not match original publication), so the story gives 1999 and does not date the first product. Shelf space: SmartCompany said in 2012 that Coles did not stock the brand, while in 2018 Smith thanked Coles and Woolworths for keeping it on shelves; the story omits this. SBS's reference to the letter sent to Coles and Woolworths and Inside Retail's to the open letter to Aldi's owners are two separate letters. The news.com.au report is cited from its syndicated copy on Newstalk ZB because thenewdaily and others block automated requests. Funding is set to 'bootstrapped': Smith owned the licensing business and no outside investors are reported. Hesiod's passage is applied by analogy; the 'two Strifes' are his own distinction between rivalry that spurs work and strife that breeds war.
